sections.h: The Letter of Jeremiah: they are not gods
sections.b: The Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6 in Catholic Bibles, a separate book in Orthodox Bibles) is the longest satire on idols outside the 66 books. Written as Jeremiah's warning to the captives going to Babylon, it expands Jeremiah 10:1–16, Isaiah 44:9–20 and Psalm 115:4–8 into a list of what the gods cannot do: they gather dust and soot, bats and cats sit on them, their priests rob them, they cannot get up when they fall, rescue the poor, send rain or set up a king, and they burn like beams in a fire. In some ten places a refrain sums up: they are not gods, so do not fear them. Its last line uses the word 'idols' for the only time: "the righteous person who keeps no idols is better off" (6:72).

common: The Letter of Jeremiah is a satire built from Jeremiah 10 and Isaiah 44, not a description of how worshipers understood their images.
uncommon: Carey Moore argued that the letter was first written in Hebrew, pointing to Greek words that look like misread Hebrew (Baruch 6:11, 6:54, 6:71); Benjamin Wright finds the evidence inconclusive.

sections.h: Gods with no work of God in them
sections.b: The Letter of Jeremiah argues for the one God almost without describing him: the gods of Babylon are "something human hands have made, and no work of God is in them" (6:50), while the sun, moon, stars, wind, clouds and fire do as God tells them (6:59–62). It never says, as Paul does in 1 Corinthians 10:20, that demons stand behind the idols.

The Letter of Jeremiah warns the captives about what they will see in Babylon: gods of silver, gold and wood carried on shoulders with crowds bowing before and behind (6:3–5), Bel brought to a mute man (6:40), and temples full of soot and bats (6:12–21). It echoes Isaiah's picture of Bel and Nebo carried off as freight (Isaiah 46:1–2).

sections.h: The Chaldeans in the Letter of Jeremiah
sections.b: The Letter of Jeremiah says "even the Chaldeans themselves dishonor" their gods, bringing Bel to a mute man as if Bel could notice (6:40–41), and denies that the gods give "signs in the sky" (6:66), the omens Babylon's scholars were famous for reading.

Besides the letter of Jeremiah 29, Greek and Latin Bibles carry a second letter in Jeremiah's name, the Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6), warning the captives against Babylon's idols. It draws on the Hebrew of Jeremiah 10 (the scarecrow of Jeremiah 10:5 is in the Hebrew, not the Greek) and replaces his seventy years with "seven generations" (6:2). Sean Adams reads it as written later in the prophet's name; Catholic and Orthodox churches receive it as Scripture.

The Letter of Jeremiah is written for exiles who will stay "as long as seven generations" (6:2): its concern is not the journey home but how to live among a foreign city's festivals without copying the foreigners or fearing their gods (6:4–5).

The Letter of Jeremiah has Jeremiah tell the captives they will be in Babylon "as long as seven generations" (6:2), far longer than the seventy years of Jeremiah 25:11 and 29:10. Daniel Harrington, counting forty years to a generation, takes it as a clue to a date about 317 BC; J. Alberto Soggin compares the problem to Daniel 9, which also rereads the seventy years; read as Jeremiah's own words, it promises a longer stay.

The Letter of Jeremiah promises the captives, "my angel is with you, and he himself is looking after your lives" (6:6), the guard of the exodus (Exodus 23:20; Exodus 32:34) sent with them into exile. The Latin Vulgate and the KJV make God himself the one who looks after them.

sections.h: Purity law as a measure of the gods
sections.b: The Letter of Jeremiah judges Babylon's cult by Israel's purity law: a woman in her monthly bleeding or just after childbirth touch the gods' sacrifices (6:28), which in Israel she could not do (Leviticus 12:4).

The Letter of Jeremiah treats the sun, moon and stars, with lightning, wind, clouds and fire, as God's servants: "when they are sent out on a task they do as they are told" (6:59). They are not gods, but they at least obey, which the idols cannot.
The Letter of Jeremiah turns Psalm 146 inside out: Babylon's gods save no one from death, give no blind man sight, and "A widow gets no mercy from them, and an orphan gets no kindness" (6:37).

The Letter of Jeremiah says the gods of Babylon will never "send rain down on people" (6:52), as Jeremiah asks, "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22); the clouds go where God orders them (6:61).
In the Letter of Jeremiah, a man may vow to the gods and never pay, and "they will never come after him for it" (6:34), the opposite of Deuteronomy 23:21, where the LORD "will surely ask it of you".
